chunks.heading: Course info: Intro to JavaScript > Teacher and class times
chunks.text: Our teacher is Ms. Rivera. Class is on Tuesday and Thursday, 4 to 6 pm, in Lab 2. Office hours are Wednesday 3 to 4 pm on Discord, in the #help channel. She answers questions there faster than by email.

chunks.heading: Course info: Intro to JavaScript > Grading
chunks.text:
- Final project: 40%
- Weekly quizzes: 30% (the lowest quiz score is dropped)
- Homework: 20%
- Participation: 10%

Late homework loses 10% per day. After 3 days it is not accepted.

chunks.heading: Course info: Intro to JavaScript > Final project
chunks.text: The final project is due Friday of week 8, before midnight. It must be a small web app that uses fetch with at least one free public API, has no frameworks (plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript only), and is deployed online with a working link. We present it in class in week 9, 5 minutes each, and we must explain one bug we fixed.

chunks.heading: Course info: Intro to JavaScript > Class rules for code
chunks.text: Ms. Rivera's rules: never use var, always use let or const. Always use === instead of ==. Every function needs a name that says what it does, like calculateTotal, not doStuff. Comment the why, not the what.

chunks.heading: Week 1: Variables and types > let and const
Week 1: Variables and types > The basic types
chunks.text:
- string: text in quotes, like "hello"
- number: 42, 3.14, also NaN ("not a number")
- boolean: true or false
- undefined: a variable that exists but has no value yet
- null: "empty on purpose", set by you
- object and array: groups of values

typeof tells you the type: typeof "hi" is "string". Weird one to remember for the quiz: typeof null is "object". It is an old bug in JavaScript that was never fixed.

chunks.heading: Week 1: Variables and types > == vs ===
chunks.text: === checks the value and the type. == converts types first, which gives surprising results: 0 == "" is true, but 0 === "" is false. That is why we always use ===.

chunks.heading: Week 1: Variables and types > Template strings
chunks.text: Use backticks to put variables inside text: `Hi ${name}, your score is ${score}`. Much cleaner than adding strings with +.

chunks.heading: Week 2: Arrays and loops > Arrays
chunks.text:
An array is an ordered list: const scores = [80, 90, 100]. Indexes start at 0, so scores[0] is 80 and scores[2] is 100. scores.length is 3, which is one more than the last index. Reading an index that does not exist, like scores[3], does not crash. It gives undefined.

Useful methods: push adds to the end, pop removes from the end, includes checks if a value is in the array, and indexOf gives the position (or -1 if it is not there).

chunks.heading: Week 2: Arrays and loops > The for loop
Week 2: Arrays and loops > Off-by-one errors
chunks.text: The most common loop bug. If you write i <= scores.length, the loop runs one extra time and reads scores[3], which is undefined. Adding undefined to a number gives NaN, so a total or an average suddenly becomes NaN. Fix: use < instead of <=. Ms. Rivera says to always check the last value i takes.

chunks.heading: Week 2: Arrays and loops > for...of
Week 2: Arrays and loops > map and filter
chunks.text: map makes a new array by changing every item: scores.map(s => s + 5). filter keeps only the items that pass a test: scores.filter(s => s >= 90). Neither changes the original array.

chunks.heading: Week 3: Functions > What a function is
Week 3: Functions > Arrow functions
chunks.text: A shorter way to write a function: const double = (n) => n * 2. With one expression, the result is returned automatically, no return keyword needed. With curly braces you must write return yourself. Forgetting return inside curly braces is a classic bug: the function gives back undefined.

chunks.heading: Week 3: Functions > Default parameters
chunks.text: You can give a parameter a default value: function greet(name = "friend"). If you call greet() with nothing, name is "friend".

chunks.heading: Week 3: Functions > Scope
chunks.text: Variables made with let or const inside a function or a block (anything in curly braces) only exist inside it. Outside, they are not defined and you get "ReferenceError: x is not defined". This is a good thing: it stops functions from changing each other's variables by accident.

chunks.heading: Week 3: Functions > Pure functions
chunks.text: A pure function always gives the same output for the same input and does not change anything outside itself. They are the easiest functions to test and debug. Try to write most of your functions this way.

chunks.heading: Week 4: Debugging > Read the error message first
chunks.text:
The error message tells you three things: the type of error, a short description, and the file and line number. Go to that line before changing anything. Most beginners skip the message and start guessing.

Common ones:
- ReferenceError: you used a name that does not exist (typo, or out of scope)
- TypeError: you used a value the wrong way, like calling something that is not a function, or reading a property of undefined
- SyntaxError: the code is not valid JavaScript, often a missing bracket or quote

chunks.heading: Week 4: Debugging > When there is no error but the result is wrong
chunks.text: Use console.log to check what a value really is at each step. Log the inputs, then the value inside the loop, then the result. The bug is between the last correct log and the first wrong one.

chunks.heading: Week 4: Debugging > Where NaN comes from
chunks.text: NaN means a math operation got something that is not a number. The usual causes: adding undefined (often from reading an array index that does not exist), dividing 0 by 0, or doing math with a string that cannot be turned into a number, like Number("abc"). NaN spreads: anything plus NaN is NaN.

chunks.heading: Week 4: Debugging > Rubber duck debugging
chunks.text: Explain your code line by line out loud, to a rubber duck or a friend. Halfway through you often hear the mistake yourself.

chunks.heading: Week 4: Debugging > Debugging with AI
chunks.text: Do not paste the error and copy the fix. Ask the AI to be a Socratic debugger: it asks you questions one at a time until you find the bug yourself. Slower once, but you remember the lesson.
